newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Legal reform crucial for Yugo banks revival.
newsitem.headline: Legal reform crucial for Yugo banks revival.

text.p: Yugoslavian banks need urgent reform but there will be no radical changes before reform of the legal system and a deal with Yugoslavia's international creditors, economists and bankers said on Wednesday.

"Our legal system protects debtors instead of creditors and as long as creditors cannot collect dues either in cash or property we will see no improvement," said Jovo Kunac, deputy general manager of Investbanka and former head of the Yugoslav Agency for Bank Rehabilitation.
Huge credit risk and massive write-offs resulted in very high commercial lending rates, running above 15 percent per month, Kunac said.

Apart from the legal reform, restoring ties with the International Monetary Fund and other creditors was the key precondition for any serious reform of the banking system which owes some $6 billion to Western creditors, he added.
Kunac insisted the size of the debt was not alarming and would be subject to rescheduling negotiations anyway.
"Once the debt deal is concluded, we would know exactly how much money is needed to rehabilitate Yugoslav banks," he added.
But foreign debt itself was less worrisome than the issue of some $4 billion in so-called old hard currency savings, frozen by the state in the early 1990s.
"This must be dealt by the state. Banks cannot solve this problem alone," Kunac said.

Economists cautioned the banking crisis was a very deep and unavoidable consequence of the existing economic system which strongly supports financial chaos leading to devastation of the banking system.

"There are big zombie banks without any credit potential. Those slowly-dying banks cause a chain-reaction and reflect on the rest of the economy," a group of economists wrote in a proposal of measures for overcoming current economic crisis.
"The first step must be to isolate highly indebted firms as well as illiquid banks from the rest of the banking system," the paper said.
To collect debt was the major headache for Yugoslav banks, operating in an economy with 23,405 companies insolvent at the end of December.
The size of their matured but unpaid liabilities stood at 5.49 billion dinars, practically matching the volume of M1 money supply of 5.5 billion dinars.
Danko Djunic, head of the Belgrade-based Economics Institute, said banks will first have to clear their balances of hard currency liabilities and write-off most bad debts before restructuring begins.
Around 100 Yugoslav commercial banks badly needed to attract more deposits, ranging between 2.5 and 3.0 billion dinars ($460 million and $550 million) at the end of 1996.
Analysts saw few ways to increase deposits in an atmosphere of distrust after 1990 foreign currency savings default.

Miloje Kanjevac, head of FINIS consulting group, said the state should allow one big foreign bank come and operate in Yugoslavia. This would attract three to five billion German marks of savings Yugoslavs hide in their mattresses.
The money would be invested in most profitable local businesses, Kanjevac said. But the state must reform its laws, so that in case of debt default creditor can seize property.
To avoid monopolist behaviour the state should limit the percentage of commission fees to the foreign bank, he said.
"Yugoslav banks are keen to accept foreign competition. It is foreign banks hesitating to come, citing the so-called outer wall of sanctions as the only excuse," Kunac said.
In the meantime, the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY), enforcing measures to restore financial discipline, said it revoked licences from two large commercial banks -- Slavija Banka and JIK Banka.
Commercial banks lose their licences if their accounts are in the red for three consecutive days or a total of seven days in one month.
"It's an anarchy to liquidate banks without any order. NBY itself owes them more than they owe to NBY. Their only sin is short-term liquidity," one outraged state banker said.

"Instead of liquidation, banks should be granted a period of three-four weeks to try to overcome liquidity problems. Only then, if they find no solution, should they be liquidated," said the banker who asked not to be named. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
